questions.stem: Decolonisation refers to:
options: the division of Germany into zones of occupation
colonies gaining independence from imperial rule
European empires expanding into Africa and Asia
settlers from a colony returning to the home country
questions.explanation: After 1945 dozens of colonies in Asia, Africa, the Middle East and the Pacific became independent states. Expansion into Africa and Asia describes the imperialism that came before.

questions.stem: Self-determination is the principle that:
options: a people has the right to choose its own government
a great power may intervene to protect its interests
a colony should be governed by a League of Nations mandate
religious leaders should hold supreme political authority
questions.explanation: Self-determination underpinned independence movements from Algeria to Timor-Leste. Rule by religious leaders is theocracy, a different idea.

questions.stem: Iran after the 1979 revolution is often described as a theocracy because:
options: the army rules the country through a council of generals
a single secular party controls every state institution
supreme authority rests with senior Islamic clergy
the Shah governed as an absolute hereditary monarch
questions.explanation: Under Khomeini's idea of guardianship of the Islamic jurist, a senior cleric became Supreme Leader with authority above elected officials. The Shah's monarchy was what the revolution overthrew.

questions.stem: After independence, a new government concentrates on setting up a civil service, courts, a tax system and a national army, rather than on promoting a common language or national symbols. This process is best described as:
options: state-building
nation-building
decolonisation
self-determination
questions.explanation: State-building means creating the institutions of government. Nation-building is different: it means creating a shared national identity, for example through a common language, symbols and history, which this government is not yet attempting.

questions.stem: A movement demanding that all people have equal rights and opportunities, whatever their race or gender, is drawing on the idea of:
options: isolationism
egalitarianism
theocracy
imperialism
questions.explanation: Egalitarianism is the belief that all people are of equal worth and should have equal rights. It drove civil rights, anti-apartheid and feminist movements alike.

questions.stem: India and Pakistan became independent in August 1947 mainly through:
options: a war of independence ending in British defeat
a referendum supervised by the United Nations
a revolution led by officers of the Indian army
negotiation with Britain, followed by partition
questions.explanation: Decades of nationalist campaigning, led by Gandhi, Nehru and Jinnah among others, ended in a negotiated British withdrawal. The subcontinent was partitioned into Hindu-majority India and Muslim-majority Pakistan.

questions.stem: Which was a short-term consequence of the partition of India in 1947?
options: mass migration and communal violence across the new borders
the immediate reunification of India and Pakistan as one state
the creation of Bangladesh as an independent nation
the return of British rule to the province of Punjab
questions.explanation: Millions of Hindus, Sikhs and Muslims fled across the new borders, and huge numbers were killed in communal violence. Bangladesh broke away from Pakistan in 1971, a long-term consequence rather than a short-term one.

questions.stem: Algeria gained independence from France in 1962 mainly through:
options: a UN decision to transfer Algeria to Moroccan rule
a vote in the French parliament before any resistance began
armed struggle led by the FLN, ended by the Évian Accords
peaceful negotiation without any fighting between the two sides
questions.explanation: The FLN fought a war from 1954 that cost hundreds of thousands of lives, before the Évian Accords led to a referendum and independence. France had regarded Algeria as part of France itself, which made it resist especially hard.

questions.stem: During the Algerian War, the French army's use of torture in the Battle of Algiers (1957) had which longer-term effect?
options: it turned French and world opinion against the war
it permanently ended FLN resistance across Algeria
it led France to grant Algeria independence that same year
it was approved by a resolution of the UN General Assembly
questions.explanation: The army defeated the FLN in the city, but revelations of torture divided France and damaged its standing abroad. Independence did not come until 1962, so the military victory did not end the struggle.

questions.stem: Who proclaimed Indonesia's independence on 17 August 1945?
options: Suharto
Ho Chi Minh
Tunku Abdul Rahman
Sukarno
questions.explanation: Sukarno and Mohammad Hatta proclaimed independence just after Japan's surrender, and the Netherlands recognised it only in 1949 after years of fighting and diplomacy. Suharto replaced Sukarno in the late 1960s.

questions.stem: Patrice Lumumba is significant in the decolonisation of the Congo as:
options: the Belgian governor who negotiated the handover of power
the army officer who later ruled the country for decades
the leader of the secession of the province of Katanga
its first Prime Minister after independence from Belgium
questions.explanation: Lumumba became Prime Minister in June 1960 but was overthrown and killed within months, amid the Congo Crisis. The army officer who later ruled for decades was Mobutu.

questions.stem: Papua New Guinea gained independence from Australia in 1975 mainly through:
options: a UN military intervention
a vote of Indonesia's parliament
peaceful negotiation
a war of independence
questions.explanation: Self-government came in 1973 and full independence on 16 September 1975, with Michael Somare as the first Prime Minister. The study design contrasts this diplomatic path with the armed struggles in Algeria and Timor-Leste.

questions.stem: Indonesia invaded East Timor (now Timor-Leste) in December 1975, shortly after:
options: Australia announced that it would annex the territory
the Netherlands handed the territory over to Indonesia
FRETILIN declared independence after Portugal's withdrawal
a UN referendum voted for integration with Indonesia
questions.explanation: Portugal left its colony in 1975, and FRETILIN declared independence on 28 November, days before the invasion. East Timor had been Portuguese, not Dutch, and its people were not consulted until 1999.

questions.stem: Why was the Santa Cruz massacre in Dili in 1991 significant for East Timorese independence?
options: it was the first time that the Timorese had resisted Indonesian rule
smuggled film of it raised world pressure on Indonesia
it ended Indonesian rule of the territory within a few weeks
it led Australia to send troops to occupy the territory at once
questions.explanation: Indonesian troops fired on mourners at a cemetery, and footage smuggled out by a foreign journalist was broadcast internationally. Resistance had been going on since 1975, and independence came only after the 1999 ballot.

questions.stem: Which was a cause of the Iranian Revolution of 1979?
options: resentment of the Shah's autocracy, secret police and US ties
a Soviet invasion of northern Iran in the year before the revolution
the Shah's introduction of strict Islamic law across Iran
the seizure of the US embassy in Tehran by Iranian students
questions.explanation: Opposition grew from clergy, students, workers and the middle class against the Shah's repression by the SAVAK and his Western-backed modernisation. The embassy seizure happened in November 1979, after the revolution, so it was a consequence.

questions.stem: While in exile, Ayatollah Khomeini spread his message inside Iran mainly through:
options: satellite television broadcasts
posts and videos on social media
an armed guerrilla army in the mountains
recorded sermons on cassette tapes
questions.explanation: Copies of his speeches on cheap cassettes were passed through mosques and markets, beyond the reach of state censorship. Social media did not exist in the 1970s; it was a key method in the Arab Spring decades later.

questions.stem: The Arab Spring began in Tunisia in December 2010 after:
options: the Egyptian army removed President Mubarak from power
a street vendor, Mohamed Bouazizi, set himself on fire in protest
NATO aircraft began bombing the forces of the Libyan government
the US-led invasion of Iraq brought down Saddam Hussein's regime
questions.explanation: Bouazizi's protest against police harassment sparked demonstrations that forced President Ben Ali to flee in January 2011. Protests then spread to Egypt, Libya, Syria, Yemen and Bahrain.

questions.stem: Which method was most closely associated with the spread of the Arab Spring protests?
options: leaflets dropped over the cities by foreign military aircraft
social media and mobile phones used to organise and share images
pirate radio stations run by exiled members of royal families
cassette tapes of sermons smuggled into the country from abroad
questions.explanation: Protesters used Facebook, Twitter and phone cameras to coordinate and to show the world what was happening. Cassette tapes were Khomeini's method in Iran in the 1970s.

questions.stem: Which statement best evaluates the extent of change brought by the Arab Spring?
options: democratic government was established in every Arab state by 2013
no ruler in any Arab country lost power as a result of the protests
the protests were confined to Tunisia and did not spread elsewhere
rulers fell in several states, but lasting democracy proved rare
questions.explanation: Long-standing rulers were removed in several states, but Egypt returned to military-backed rule and Libya, Syria and Yemen fell into civil war. Evaluating extent means weighing real change against strong continuity.

questions.stem: Terrorism is best defined as:
options: economic sanctions imposed on a country by the United Nations
violence or threats against civilians for political aims
open warfare between the armed forces of two sovereign states
deliberate non-violent law-breaking to protest an unjust law
questions.explanation: Terrorist groups aim to spread fear among a wider population to force political change. Non-violent law-breaking is civil disobedience, a very different method.

questions.stem: Which was a short-term consequence of the 11 September 2001 attacks?
options: the founding of Al Qaeda by Osama bin Laden
the US-led invasion of Afghanistan in October 2001
the end of the Cold War and the breakup of the USSR
the Gulf War to drive Iraqi forces out of Kuwait
questions.explanation: The USA and its allies, including Australia, invaded Afghanistan to remove the Taliban, who had sheltered Al Qaeda. The Gulf War was in 1991 and Al Qaeda was founded in the late 1980s, so neither can be a consequence.

questions.stem: The Bali bombings of 12 October 2002, which killed 202 people including 88 Australians, were carried out by:
options: the Tamil Tigers
Hezbollah
Jemaah Islamiyah
FRETILIN
questions.explanation: Jemaah Islamiyah, a group linked to Al Qaeda, bombed nightclubs in Kuta. The attack brought the 'war on terror' close to home for Australians and led to closer counter-terrorism cooperation with Indonesia.

questions.stem: The attack at the 1972 Munich Olympics, in which Israeli athletes and coaches were killed, was carried out by:
options: the Japanese Red Army, a revolutionary group
Black September, a Palestinian militant group
the Baader-Meinhof group of West Germany
ETA, which fought for an independent Basque state
questions.explanation: Black September took Israeli team members hostage to demand the release of Palestinian prisoners, and eleven Israeli team members were killed. The attack was seen live on television, showing how terrorism sought a global audience.

questions.stem: Apartheid in South Africa, introduced by the National Party government from 1948, was:
options: an alliance of African states against colonialism
a system of laws enforcing racial segregation
a policy of gradual transition to majority rule
a British colonial law repealed at independence
questions.explanation: Laws classified every person by race and controlled where they could live, work, travel and marry, keeping power in white hands. It lasted until the early 1990s.

questions.stem: Why was the Sharpeville massacre of March 1960 a turning point in the struggle against apartheid?
options: the ANC and PAC were banned and turned towards armed resistance
it led the government to release Nelson Mandela from prison
it forced the government to abolish the pass laws that same year
it brought majority rule to South Africa within a single year
questions.explanation: Police killed 69 people protesting against the pass laws, and the government then banned the main African nationalist organisations. Unable to protest legally, the ANC formed an armed wing, Umkhonto we Sizwe, in 1961.

questions.stem: The Soweto uprising of June 1976 began as a protest by school students against:
options: being taught in Afrikaans
the imprisonment of Nelson Mandela
the banning of the ANC
the closure of their schools
questions.explanation: Students marched against a rule that some subjects be taught in Afrikaans, seen as the language of the oppressor, and police opened fire. The uprising spread across the country and drew international condemnation.

questions.stem: Which is an example of international pressure on South Africa's apartheid government?
options: the Rivonia Trial of Nelson Mandela and others
the Soweto uprising by school students
the formation of the armed wing of the ANC
sporting boycotts and economic sanctions
questions.explanation: Countries, including Australia, cut sporting ties with apartheid South Africa, and many imposed trade and investment sanctions. The other three were events inside South Africa, either resistance or the state's response to it.

questions.stem: Apartheid ended with South Africa's first democratic elections in April 1994, in which:
options: only white South Africans were allowed to vote
Desmond Tutu was elected as the new President
the ANC won and Nelson Mandela became President
the National Party won a majority of the seats
questions.explanation: Millions of Black South Africans voted for the first time, and Mandela became the country's first Black President. Tutu later chaired the Truth and Reconciliation Commission.

questions.stem: The Northern Ireland Civil Rights Association, formed in 1967, campaigned mainly against:
options: the partition of India and Pakistan by the British government
discrimination against Protestants in the police and courts
discrimination against Catholics in housing, jobs and voting
the presence of the Irish army in the six counties of Ulster
questions.explanation: Inspired by the US civil rights movement, it used marches to demand fair treatment for the Catholic minority under a unionist government. Violent responses to its marches helped begin the Troubles.

questions.stem: The Good Friday Agreement of 1998 is significant because it:
options: ended British involvement in Northern Ireland entirely
set up power-sharing between unionists and nationalists
united Northern Ireland with the Republic of Ireland
banned every party with links to paramilitary groups
questions.explanation: The agreement created a power-sharing Assembly and stated that Northern Ireland's status could change only with the consent of a majority of its people. Northern Ireland remained part of the United Kingdom.

questions.stem: The genocide in Rwanda in 1994 was directed mainly against:
options: the Hutu majority of the population
Belgian settlers and their families
foreign aid workers and missionaries
the Tutsi minority and moderate Hutu
questions.explanation: Hutu extremists, using radio propaganda and militias, killed huge numbers of Tutsi and Hutu who opposed them over about one hundred days. The Tutsi-led Rwandan Patriotic Front ended the genocide by taking power.

questions.stem: Which best describes the international response to the Rwandan genocide while it was happening?
options: the UN cut its peacekeeping force rather than reinforcing it
NATO launched air strikes against the Hutu extremist militias
the USA sent a large force of troops to protect Tutsi civilians
a large new UN force stopped the killing within the first week
questions.explanation: After ten Belgian peacekeepers were killed, the Security Council reduced the UN mission to a small force, and the major powers avoided calling the killing genocide. This failure is a key example of the limits of the UN.

questions.stem: Which is an example of an established power resisting challenge through repression?
options: the result of the 1967 referendum in Australia
the Évian Accords between France and the FLN
the banning of the ANC and jailing of its leaders
the signing of the Good Friday Agreement in 1998
questions.explanation: The apartheid government tried to keep white minority rule by outlawing opposition and imprisoning leaders such as Mandela. The other three were agreements or reforms that accepted at least some change.

questions.stem: The Montgomery Bus Boycott of 1955–56 began after Rosa Parks:
options: refused to give up her bus seat to a white passenger
was elected as the first Black mayor of Montgomery
led the March on Washington for jobs and freedom
won a Supreme Court case ending segregated schools
questions.explanation: Parks was arrested, and Black residents refused to ride the city's buses for over a year until the Supreme Court ruled bus segregation unconstitutional. The boycott brought Martin Luther King Jr to national leadership.

questions.stem: Which best shows the limits of the change achieved by the US civil rights movement by the late 1960s?
options: legal segregation ended, but poverty and informal discrimination remained
the Civil Rights Act was defeated in Congress and segregation stayed lawful
African Americans in the South were still legally barred from voting
the Supreme Court restored the principle of 'separate but equal'
questions.explanation: The Civil Rights Act of 1964 and the Voting Rights Act of 1965 ended legal segregation and protected voting, but inequality in housing, jobs and income remained. This is why historians weigh change against continuity.

questions.stem: The 1965 Freedom Ride through country New South Wales, led by Charles Perkins, aimed to:
options: expose racism against Aboriginal people in country towns
demand the return of traditional lands to the Gurindji people
protest against Australia's commitment of troops to Vietnam
win equal pay for Aboriginal stockmen in the cattle industry
questions.explanation: University students travelled by bus to towns such as Walgett and Moree, drawing media attention to segregated swimming pools, clubs and cinemas. The Gurindji land claim began with the Wave Hill walk-off in 1966.

questions.stem: The 1967 referendum, approved by more than 90 per cent of voters, changed the Constitution so that:
options: Aboriginal land rights were recognised across all of the states and territories
Aboriginal people became Australian citizens with the same legal status as others
the Commonwealth could make laws for Aboriginal people and count them in the census
Aboriginal people gained the right to vote in federal elections for the first time
questions.explanation: The referendum removed the words excluding Aboriginal people from Commonwealth law-making power and repealed the section excluding them from the census. Federal voting rights had come in 1962, and citizenship did not depend on the referendum.

questions.stem: The Gurindji walk-off from Wave Hill station in 1966, led by Vincent Lingiari, began over wages and conditions and became a campaign for:
options: an end to the White Australia policy
a treaty with the British government
the return of their traditional lands
the right to vote in federal elections
questions.explanation: The Gurindji's long strike became a land rights claim, and in 1975 Prime Minister Gough Whitlam returned part of their land. It helped lead to the Aboriginal Land Rights (Northern Territory) Act 1976.

questions.stem: The High Court's Mabo decision of 1992 was significant because it:
options: ended the White Australia immigration policy
rejected terra nullius and recognised native title
gave Aboriginal people the vote in federal elections
led directly to the holding of the 1967 referendum
questions.explanation: The court accepted Eddie Mabo's claim that the Meriam people held their land under their own law, rejecting the idea that Australia had belonged to no one. Parliament then passed the Native Title Act 1993.

questions.stem: The Stonewall Riots of June 1969 in New York began when:
options: protesters marched against the Vietnam War draft
students occupied a university building in Manhattan
workers struck for equal pay in the city's factories
police raided a gay bar and its patrons fought back
questions.explanation: Resistance to the raid on the Stonewall Inn led to days of protest and is seen as a turning point for the gay liberation movement. Anniversary marches became the first pride marches.

questions.stem: Second-wave feminism in the 1960s and 1970s focused on issues such as:
options: the abolition of slavery in the southern United States
the right of men to vote without a property qualification
equal pay, workplace discrimination and reproductive rights
the vote, which most women in the West did not yet have
questions.explanation: Most Western women already had the vote, the goal of first-wave feminism, so the second wave targeted inequality at work, in law and at home. Books such as Betty Friedan's The Feminine Mystique (1963) helped spark it.

questions.stem: In 1965 Merle Thornton and Rosalie Bognor chained themselves to the bar of a Brisbane hotel to protest against:
options: the closure of hotels at six o'clock
the exclusion of women from public bars
unequal pay for women in the public service
Australia's involvement in the Vietnam War
questions.explanation: Women were not served in the public bars of Queensland hotels, and the protest used civil disobedience to draw media attention to everyday discrimination. It is an example of the direct action of the women's movement.

questions.stem: The Tiananmen Square pro-democracy protests in Beijing ended when:
options: UN peacekeepers arrived to separate the two sides
the army cleared the square by force on 3–4 June 1989
the Communist Party agreed to hold free elections
the students left after Deng Xiaoping resigned
questions.explanation: After weeks of protest and a declaration of martial law, troops and tanks moved into central Beijing and killed many civilians. Deng remained China's dominant leader.

questions.stem: Which best describes the outcome of the 1989 pro-democracy movement in China?
options: China's leaders resigned and handed power to the student leaders
the party kept its monopoly on power while pursuing market reform
multiparty elections were introduced within the following decade
economic reform was abandoned and private markets were shut down
questions.explanation: Political continuity was enforced by repression, while economic reform resumed in the early 1990s. The movement's demands for political change were not achieved.

questions.stem: The campaign against the Franklin Dam in Tasmania succeeded in 1983 when:
options: the High Court upheld federal power to stop the dam
the Tasmanian Parliament voted unanimously to abandon the dam
the United Nations ordered Tasmania to cancel construction
the companies building the dam collapsed into bankruptcy
questions.explanation: The Commonwealth relied on its external affairs power and the World Heritage Convention, and the High Court ruled in its favour. The blockade and national campaign made the environment a major political issue.
